situation: I'm the on-call engineering lead at a B2B payments startup. I must explain a six-hour outage to the VP of Ops and the procurement lead at our largest customer, who are considering ending the contract.

scenario.title: Six-Hour Outage: Keeping the Largest Customer
scenario.setting: A tense video call the morning after a six-hour payments outage. You are meeting with the VP of Operations and the procurement lead from your largest customer to explain what happened and discuss the contract.
scenario.user_role: You are the on-call engineering lead at a B2B payments startup, meeting to explain a six-hour outage to your largest customer.
scenario.user_goal: Explain what happened during the outage clearly, rebuild trust, and persuade the customer not to end the contract.
user_knows: You are speaking with the VP of Ops and the procurement lead from your largest customer
The customer is considering ending the contract

cast.name: Diane Mercer
cast.role: VP of Operations at the customer
cast.appearance: Mid-40s, sharp blazer, tired and tense after an overnight escalation
cast.goal: Protect her operations and team from another failure and get a credible operational guarantee, not vague technical excuses
cast.secret: Her team manually reconciled 430 failed payments overnight and she already promised her CEO this was a one-time event
cast.reveal_when: asks what her team had to do during the six hours to keep operations running
red_lines: Will not accept blame shifted to her team
Will not accept vague reassurances with no concrete prevention plan
cast.history: You've been her technical contact through monthly ops check-ins since they became your largest account. Your last exchange was your brief incident alert late last night promising a full explanation on this call.

cast.name: Marcus Webb
cast.appearance: Early 30s, business casual, calm with a notebook open
cast.voice: Polite but transactional, focused on terms and leverage
cast.goal: Use the outage to extract commercial protection or a clean exit option, focusing on contract terms rather than technical details
cast.secret: He has a signed competing vendor quote that is 15% cheaper and must make a renewal recommendation to finance by Friday
cast.reveal_when: asks directly what commercial terms would be needed to keep the contract
red_lines: Will not agree to continue without concrete protections
Will not be brushed off on SLA and contract questions
cast.history: You met him once during last quarter's contract expansion when he pressed you on SLA penalties. Your last exchange was his short email this morning forwarding the uptime terms before this meeting.

scenario.opening_line: Thanks for getting on this. You promised us answers last night, so walk us through those six hours yesterday — my team felt every minute of it — and why we should stay with you.

events.description: Diane gets an urgent message from her CEO and says she only has 10 more minutes, demanding clear answers fast.
Marcus notes that end-users are complaining about the outage publicly on social media, raising reputational pressure.

success_criteria: Takes clear ownership of the outage without minimizing or deflecting blame
Explains the cause and impact in clear language a non-engineer can understand
Offers a specific remediation and follow-up plan that addresses prevention and contract concerns
